To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
weight regain in diabetic and normal glucose-tolerants is associated with increased fat mass and reduced fat oxidation.

weight regain in both diabetic and normoglucemic obese adults was accompanied by a decrease in basal fat oxidation and insulin-mediated fat oxidation, and a significant increase in fasting insulin levels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of weight regain on substrate metabolism, body composition and metabolic parameters in normal glucose tolerant and type II diabetes obese adults.
the effects of weight regain on substrate oxidation and metabolic health in obese individuals.
the effects of weight loss on the metabolic and physiological parameters of obese subjects with and without type II diabetes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
weight regain after weight loss is associated with reduced basal fat oxidation, increased fat mass, and reduced insulin sensitivity, irrespective of the presence or absence of diabetes.

the metabolic abnormalities that are associated with obesity, such as insulin resistance and dyslipidaemia are not necessarily a consequence of weight regain but rather of the metabolic abnormalities that were present prior to weight loss.
the metabolic response to fat regain is similar in NGT and DM subjects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

weight regain after weight loss, and the development of fasting hyperinsulineamia, is associated with a reduced ability to suppress fat oxidation and an increased capacity to oxidise carbohydrate, in both NGT, and DM obese adults.
fat regain is associated with a loss of metabolic flexibility, which is not different between diabetic and normoglcaemic obese adults.
in both NGT subjects and those with type 2 diabetes, fat regain and fasting glucose and insulin levels are associated with reduced fat oxidation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
both groups regained weight and were not different in any of the metabolic parameters at 5 years after significant weight loss.
both NGT and diabetic obese adults are at risk of developing the metabolic syndrome with fat regain, with the DM subjects more insulin resistant than the NGT subjects.
